In the language itself, su‘luk means a poor person. The well-known Arab sa‘alik were poor men who emerged from the social divisions discussed above. They broke away from their tribes as an expression of grievance and rebellion, and as a way to escape the poverty they suffered. Most were poor and often had nothing to eat. If they gained something through a raid or similar action, the tribal chief took the lion’s share of the booty, leaving them only scraps. See Ahmad Amin, “Su‘luk Life and Chivalry in Islam,” Iqra’ series, no. 1, 1952, p. 27. al-Qattal al-Kilabi described their condition in lines including:↩︎

In pre-Islamic terminology, an ashira is a group of tribes that all trace themselves to one genealogical origin, as Quraysh did. Quraysh consisted of several tribal branches but together formed one ashira. The upper group—the Qurayshi commercial aristocracy—contained members from about ten of these branches.↩︎

The well-known term mala’ of Mecca draws its historical meaning from its linguistic sense. Dictionaries define it as the nobles, leading men, and people of distinction—that is, people marked by status, appearance, and honor. See al-Qamus al-Muhit, section on hamza, chapter on m, entry “mala’”; and Lisan al-Arab, pp. 154–155. al-Munjid gives a vivid definition: “The mala’: the leading men of the people, those who fill the eyes with splendor and the chest with awe.” See al-Munjid, letter m, entry “mala’.”↩︎

In the terminology of pre-Islamic history, Ahabish refers to a group of dark-skinned slaves of African origin. The name came from the chroniclers’ belief that they were Ethiopian in origin. Wealthy Meccans used them for various kinds of labor and service. See Lammens, Western Arabia before the Hijra, pp. 244–245; and Jawad Ali, vol. 4, p. 198.↩︎

See Lammens, “The Ahabish and the Military System in Mecca,” al-Mashriq, Beirut, year 34, 1936, pp. 1, 527; and al-Baladhuri, Genealogies, vol. 1, p. 85. Al-Baladhuri reports an incident showing that the Ka‘ba was sometimes raided in attempts to steal the valuables it contained. He says that three men from Quraysh came one morning to the door of the Ka‘ba, which had plates of gold attached to it, and stole it. This report, which al-Baladhuri traces to Ibn Abbas, together with Lammens’s research, suggests that robbery of the Ka‘ba was familiar enough—not only for stealing a gold-plated door, but also for stealing wealth stored there by rich Meccans.↩︎

These public functions existed in the pre-Islamic period, except for the council assembly. Pre-Islamic custom assigned them to whoever held tribal leadership in Mecca. The hijaba meant keeping the keys of the Ka‘ba and opening its doors for pilgrims during religious seasons. The siqaya meant filling leather water basins for pilgrims in the courtyard of the Ka‘ba. The rifada meant feeding needy pilgrims during the days of pilgrimage. The liwa’ was the office of carrying or raising the war banner before the fighters when needed. Mecca also had the office of military command, meaning leadership of the army in war. See Ibn Hisham, Life of the Prophet, vol. 1, pp. 132, 137.↩︎
Here mawdu‘ means annulled—something for which no compensation or legal claim, such as blood money, is due. One says “the offense was set aside for so-and-so,” meaning it was cancelled.↩︎

The verb sharaha can mean to break the head, and one may also say it of striking a person at the neck. The use here is therefore figurative: every claim or penalty arising from bloodshed is smashed and cut down beneath Qusayy’s feet, so that no claim or penalty remains against him.↩︎

The dir‘ of a young girl, like a covering, was a small garment she wore in her family home. When she reached young womanhood, this garment was removed and she was dressed in the woman’s dir‘, a larger dress worn in the home. It seems that in the pre-Islamic period this change was marked by a ceremony.↩︎

The chroniclers often become confused and contradict themselves on this subject. They greatly exaggerate the illiteracy and ignorance of the pre-Islamic Arabs and their lack of reading and writing. Yet they also admit that when Islam appeared there were seventeen people in Mecca who could write, while claiming that Yemen did not have even one writer—despite the evidence contradicting both claims. At the same time, they speak of alliances whose agreements and charters were written down, such as the alliance between Banu Khuza‘a and Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, which they say was recorded in Dar al-Nadwa. See al-Baladhuri, Genealogies, vol. 1, p. 71; and Ibn Sa‘d, Classes, vol. 1, p. 81. They also write at length about the poetic and oratorical skill of the pre-Islamic Arabs, which itself contradicts the picture they give of total intellectual deprivation. Another contradiction is that while denying outright that the pre-Islamic Arabs knew reading and writing, they point to Qur’anic texts showing the opposite—texts indicating that reading and writing were familiar in the late pre-Islamic period. The Qur’an uses many forms of the words for reading and writing and words referring to writing materials and tools, such as ink, pens, scroll, and sheet. Izzat Darwaza, in The Age of the Prophet, p. 269, counted more than three hundred words of this kind.↩︎

It is historically established that pre-Islamic inscriptions used two main scripts. The first was the Musnad script, used for Minaean, Sabaean, Qatabanian, Himyarite, and Awsanian inscriptions, all in South Arabian dialects. The second was the Nabataean script, derived from late Aramaic, and used in the only pre-Islamic inscriptions that have reached us and are referred to here. Thamudic, Safaitic, and Lihyanite inscriptions were written in scripts derived from Musnad. Musnad is older than the Nabataean script, and inscriptions discovered in the Arabian Peninsula show that it was widely used in Arabia both before and after the beginning of the Common Era. See Jawad Ali, vol. 7, pp. 36–37.↩︎

This is Jadhima ibn Malik, one of the earliest Tanukhid kings of al-Hira, known by the titles al-Abrash and al-Waddah. The chroniclers say that al-Zabba’, queen of Palmyra, killed him in revenge for her father Amr ibn Zarib. See al-Tabari, vol. 2, p. 32.↩︎
The text is called the Namara inscription after the place where it was discovered, in the Hawran mountains of Syria.↩︎

This is Imru’ al-Qays I, one of the Lakhmid kings of al-Hira, known by the title al-Muharriq or Muharriq, a title later associated with Banu Nasr. al-Tabari says of this Imru’ al-Qays that he was one of the Persian governors and rulers over the frontier Arabs of Rabi‘a, Nasr, and others from the deserts of Iraq, the Hijaz, and the Jazira. al-Tabari, vol. 2, pp. 64–65.↩︎

The date at the end of the inscription follows the old Bosra calendar, which begins with Roman control of the Bosra region as a Roman province in 105 CE. Adding 105 to the number 223 written in the inscription gives 328 CE as the year of the death of Imru’ al-Qays I.↩︎

Lihyan and Thamud were two tribes or peoples—the word sha‘b, with a short i, means a large tribal group—living in western Arabia before the Common Era. Each established a local government after the collapse of Minaean and Sabaean rule in the Hijaz. Both used writing derived from the South Arabian Musnad script and spoke North Arabian dialects. As for the Safaitic people, their name comes from the al-Safa region of Syria, where Orientalists found ancient inscriptions. Similar inscriptions were also discovered elsewhere in the Syrian desert and upper Hijaz, and all were called Safaitic inscriptions after al-Safa to distinguish them from inscriptions named after other places where some of them were found.↩︎

Another reason should be added for the loss of some pre-Islamic poetry: Islam’s cautious attitude toward poetry that preserved pagan ideas or remnants of tribal fanaticism. Umar ibn al-Khattab was known to deal strictly with poets whose verse violated Islamic norms. It is also said that he increased the stipend of the poet Labid when he learned that Labid had stopped composing poetry. See Ibn Sallam, Classes of Poets, pp. 25, 30, 32, 42.↩︎

There is abundant historical evidence for this. One example is enough here. Ibn Sallam says of Quraysh that they looked at their share of poetry and found it small in the pre-Islamic period, so in Islam they increased it greatly. By “increased it,” he means that large amounts of poetry were fabricated and attributed to the pre-Islamic period. See Classes of Poets, p. 62; and the same source, p. 10.↩︎

See, for example, al-Aghani, Bulaq ed., vol. 1, p. 30. Abu al-Faraj then gives the verses Abd al-Aziz ibn Nahshal composed for this purpose.↩︎
See Ibn Hisham, Life of the Prophet, vol. 1, pp. 18–26, 5–53, and elsewhere.↩︎

There are many examples showing that early scholars were aware of this problem. One is enough to stand for them all. al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi says that Hammad al-Rawiya corrupted Arabic poetry. He explains that Hammad knew the dialects of the Arabs, their poetry, the styles of their poets, and their meanings. Because of this knowledge, he could compose poetry closely resembling the style of an earlier, pre-Islamic poet, attribute it to that poet, and then spread it widely under that name. In this way, al-Dabbi says, the poetry of the Arabs became mixed together, and only a critical expert could distinguish the authentic from the false—and where could such an expert be found? Taha Husayn wrote in the introduction to the second edition: “This is last year’s book. One chapter has been removed, one retained, other chapters added, and the title has been changed slightly.” He did not explain what had been removed, retained, or added, or why the changes were made. In fact, what was removed was the first chapter on method. But the chapter was not really deleted except in two senses. First, it no longer appeared as the opening chapter. Second, certain phrases and words were changed, especially passages touching on some Islamic beliefs. The substance of the chapter, after revision, was divided between two new chapters: “Literature and Its History” and “The Pre-Islamic Arabs: Their Language and Literature.” He also added passages to the beginning and end of the chapter applying his method to some pre-Islamic poets, and added two chapters at the end of the book, one on the nature and forms of pre-Islamic poetry and one on pre-Islamic prose. These revisions were not made by his own free choice. He was forced into them after a campaign of intellectual and material intimidation led by rigid conservatives among Azhar scholars, university academics, and literary figures, along with members of the royal court pursuing political aims. Despite all of this, the basic argument and method of the book did not change.↩︎
